intelligence.partsAvailability: Mechanical components remain supportable; aging teak and hotel systems dominate refit exposure.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Established but older used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A larger traditional Albin Taiwan trawler with two private cabins, full walkaround decks, teak-rich interior and well-protected running gear, providing liveaboard-scale comfort while retaining economical semi-displacement cruising.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A lot of traditional cruising yacht for the money, but exterior teak, twin engines on most examples, two heads and larger hotel systems make upkeep firmly yacht-scale. Full walkaround decks are a practical advantage over the Sundeck sistership.
designLineage: The Albin 40 Trawler was produced from 1987–1993.
Its sistership, the Albin 40 Sundeck, uses the same basic hull and interior but substitutes a full-width raised aft deck for the Trawler's walkaround arrangement.
The 40 belongs to the same traditional Asian-built trawler branch as the Albin 36, not the later U.S. Tournament Express/Family Cruiser line.
Single Lehman power existed, but most 40s were sold with twin Lehmans or later Cummins diesels.

intelligence.signature: Compact full-displacement raised-pilothouse cruiser with true long-range economy.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Use a heavily ballasted double-ended hull and minimal horsepower to create a small boat that behaves more like a little ship than a fast cruiser.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple comfortable at six knots who values range, simplicity and offshore-capable hull form more than speed or open side decks.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Perkins-era mechanical knowledge remains broad and the owner group is unusually strong; model-specific windows, tanks and joinery are largely custom work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Very limited but enthusiast-supported used market; 29 Voyagers were built.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The roomiest powerboat version of Willard's famous Vega 30 displacement hull: a compact raised-pilothouse cruiser with a full-width salon, single Perkins diesel, ballasted keel and genuine passagemaker-style fuel economy at about six knots.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Extremely simple and economical by modern standards: one low-powered diesel, shaft drive, large tanks and few hotel systems. The main ownership challenge is age—original black-iron fuel tanks, windows, wiring, plywood-cored/sheathed superstructure and decades of owner modifications can dominate refit cost.
designLineage: The Hale Field-designed Vega 30 family was produced from 1972–1975, with 110 hulls across Searcher, Voyager, Nomad and Horizon configurations.
The Voyager was the raised-pilothouse version and the owners registry records 29 examples.

The Voyager shares the same full-displacement, ballasted Vega 30 hull with the other power variants, but its full-width salon and raised pilothouse make it a genuine configuration distinction rather than a duplicate.
The later Willard 30/4 Mark IV was derived primarily from the Vega 30 Nomad, not from the Voyager.

evidence.claim: Model character and lineage researched from Willard owners-registry history, factory manuals/brochures and surviving hull records.

intelligence.signature: Bill Garden's pioneering production-fiberglass full-displacement trawler in its dominant Standard Cruiser form.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Translate commercial double-ended trawler proportions into a durable fiberglass recreational cruiser with ballast, protected running gear and very low continuous fuel burn.
intelligence.idealOwner: A classic-boat buyer who wants authentic displacement-cruiser behavior and accepts substantial age-related stewardship.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Generic diesel and marine systems remain supportable; original 1960s Willard-specific fittings and structure are restoration work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Extremely small surviving fleet; only 39 Vega 36 hulls of all configurations were produced.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The original production-fiberglass Willard trawler: a Bill Garden-designed double-ended full-displacement cruiser with a ballasted keel, single diesel, flybridge sedan layout and unusually serious offshore proportions for a 36-footer.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A remarkably substantial old fiberglass cruiser with simple single-diesel machinery and excellent displacement efficiency. Its age is the central issue: tankage, original electrical systems, windows, deck hardware and more than sixty years of repairs or modifications require careful hull-specific inspection.
designLineage: Bill Garden designed the Vega 36 in 1961 for Vega Marine, with construction subcontracted to Willard Boat Works.
Hulls 1–25 were marketed as Vega 36s; after Willard acquired the mold, later hulls were marketed as Willard Vega 36s.
Thirty-nine hulls were produced through 1970: 28 Standard Cruisers, 6 Aft Pilothouse boats, 5 motorsailers and one full sailing version according to the owner archive.
B-Atlas now uses the Standard Cruiser as the canonical powerboat identity because the prior generic 'Vega 36 family' record mixed materially different power and sail configurations.

evidence.claim: Model character and lineage researched from Willard owners-registry history, factory manuals/brochures and surviving hull records.

intelligence.signature: Rare widebody Vega 40 flybridge sedan built before Willard's 1977 molded-superstructure redesign.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Scale the Vega displacement philosophy into two-stateroom liveaboard volume, sacrificing side decks to maximize interior width.
intelligence.idealOwner: An experienced classic-trawler buyer who prioritizes interior volume and rarity over easy deck circulation or standardized parts.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mainstream machinery can be supported, but virtually all model-specific structure, glazing and interior components are custom due to the three-boat production run.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Exceptionally rare; only three Nomads are documented.
intelligence.characterNarrative: An exceptionally rare widebody flybridge sedan from Willard's early Vega 40 family, using a full-displacement hull, two-stateroom/two-head interior and no side decks to maximize living space in a traditional long-range cruiser.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Large living space and full-displacement efficiency are attractive, but scarcity means nearly every assumption must be verified on the individual hull. Lack of side decks, vintage systems, plywood-era superstructure construction and limited model-specific parts make condition more important than nominal specification.
designLineage: The Vega 40 was introduced in 1973 as the larger replacement for the Vega 36.
The early 1973–1977 Vega 40 family consisted of Nomad flybridge sedans, Voyager raised-pilothouse boats and one motorsailer.
Only three Vega 40 Nomads were built, and the Nomad used a widebody salon without walkaround side decks.
In 1977 Willard replaced the early Vega 40 with a new molded-superstructure 40; the later Flybridge Sedan regained side decks and should not be conflated with the Vega 40 Nomad.

evidence.claim: Model character and lineage researched from Willard owners-registry history, factory manuals/brochures and surviving hull records.

intelligence.signature: Tiny trailerable Ted Brewer pocket trawler with outboard-in-well simplicity.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Deliver genuine cruising accommodation, protected helm and extreme fuel economy in the smallest practical trailerable package.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple happy with very compact living who wants inexpensive canal, river, lake and sheltered-coastal cruising.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Excellent for generic outboard and marine components; builder-specific trim and fittings depend on owner fabrication or used parts.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but persistent enthusiast market with roughly 130 boats reportedly built.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A genuinely tiny Ted Brewer-designed pocket trawler built around simplicity, highway trailering and protected-water cruising. The Nomad uses a single outboard in a well, an 8'6" beam, shallow draft and a compact pilothouse/cabin arrangement to provide surprising cruising utility at roughly seven knots.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Among the simplest cruising boats in B-Atlas: one small outboard, modest electrical and plumbing systems, shallow draft and true trailerability. The principal risks are age, trailer condition, water intrusion, old wiring and owner modifications rather than propulsion complexity.
designLineage: The Nimble Nomad was designed by Ted Brewer and entered production around 1990.
Owner records identify approximately 130 boats built, making the Nomad the most numerous of Nimble's power-cruiser designs.
The outboard-in-well arrangement and shallow, easily trailered hull distinguish it from Nimble's later diesel-powered Wanderer.
Ted Brewer himself owned a Nomad for years, reinforcing that the design was intended as a practical small cruising boat rather than a novelty.

evidence.claim: Model character and lineage researched from period reviews, owner records and Ted Brewer/Nimble owner references.

intelligence.signature: Trailer-width raised-pilothouse diesel trawler with serious cruising systems in a very compact hull.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Provide the feel, finish and machinery access of a larger pilothouse trawler while keeping beam at legal trailer width and maintaining efficient single-diesel operation.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple wanting a real pilothouse and shaft-drive diesel in the smallest practical transportable package.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong current North Pacific support plus mainstream Cummins and marine equipment; the discontinued 28 still benefits from active builder knowledge.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Scarce used model, but highly recognizable among pocket-trawler buyers.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A purpose-built pocket trawler that combines a legal-width 8'6" beam, raised pilothouse, warm teak interior and single Cummins shaft drive in a genuinely transportable package. It cruises efficiently at 6–8 knots but uses a modified semi-displacement version of Karl Stambaugh's original full-displacement concept to reach roughly 10–13 knots when needed.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A strong owner-operator design with single-shaft diesel propulsion, bow thruster, excellent machinery access for the size and little exterior wood. Trailerability is real in beam, but total rig weight, length and height demand serious tow equipment rather than casual SUV trailering.
designLineage: North Pacific Yachts was founded in 2004 by John and Trevor Brice; the 28 became the company's third model.
Trevor Brice developed the NP28 after seeing Karl Stambaugh's Trailer Trawler 28 concept in Passagemaker in 2007.
Stambaugh's original concept was full displacement; North Pacific modified the hull slightly to semi-displacement to increase maximum speed.
The first China-built NP28 hull arrived in 2009, establishing a distinct compact branch below North Pacific's larger pilothouse and sedan cruisers.

evidence.claim: Model character and lineage researched from North Pacific-hosted period reviews, builder history and model-specific sea trials.

intelligence.signature: Europa-style single-diesel sedan designed explicitly around owner feedback for protected decks and one-level living.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Combine classic sedan-trawler circulation with modern semi-displacement construction, accessible machinery and economical long-range operation.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple planning extended Pacific Northwest, Great Loop or similar coastal cruising who values protected deck access and single-engine economy.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong current builder support and mainstream Cummins systems; model-specific documentation remains accessible through North Pacific.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but established used fleet with strong brand recognition in the Pacific Northwest.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A traditional Europa-style sedan trawler interpreted through North Pacific's modern semi-displacement construction: one-level salon/galley/lower helm, covered walkaround decks, large cockpit, command bridge and a single protected Cummins diesel intended for economical long-distance coastal cruising.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Designed for hands-on cruising couples: wide protected decks, single diesel, accessible systems and substantial tankage reduce operational stress. It is nevertheless a 24,000-pound yacht with flybridge, heating, thrusters and significant hotel systems, so annual ownership is materially beyond pocket-trawler scale.
designLineage: The first North Pacific 38 Sedan was delivered to North America in early 2010.
The 38 was created after owner feedback requested a salon, galley and helm on one level plus covered walkaround side decks.
North Pacific openly credited classic CHB sedan trawlers as inspiration, while giving the 38 a larger beam, longer hull and modern fiberglass construction.
The 38 uses a new mold but draws its semi-displacement hull philosophy from the company's earlier North Pacific 39 and 43 pilothouse models.

intelligence.signature: Small U.S.-built full-displacement DeFever passagemaker with single-Lehman simplicity.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Put offshore trawler hull proportions and secure deck access into a couple-sized 34-footer.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting authentic displacement behavior and classic trawler character in the smallest DeFever package.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Lehman-era systems are widely understood; original DeFever-specific fittings are scarce.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but recognized collector/enthusiast market.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A compact U.S.-built Arthur DeFever full-displacement passagemaker with serious trawler proportions, wide side decks and a single Lehman diesel. The 34 is unusually small for DeFever but retains the deep keel, flared bow and offshore-oriented hull character that defined his early cruising designs.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Very simple mechanically and efficient at seven knots, with a single Lehman and accessible engine room. Age-related tanks, windows, deck hardware and teak are the dominant ownership risks; the small U.S.-built production run makes original model-specific fittings uncommon.
designLineage: The 34 Passagemaker was built in California rather than Taiwan and represents one of the few U.S.-built DeFever production trawlers.
It carries the same deep-keel, full-displacement philosophy that grew from Arthur DeFever's commercial tuna-clipper work and early Offshore Cruising Society designs.
The 34 is a sedan couple's cruiser rather than a scaled-down aft-cabin DeFever.
DeFever Cruisers and Powerboat Guide both identify it as a distinct 1974–1976 production model.

intelligence.signature: Early wooden DeFever full-displacement passagemaker from the original offshore-cruiser era.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Adapt commercial tuna-clipper seaworthiness into private long-range power cruising before fiberglass production became standard.
intelligence.idealOwner: An experienced wooden-boat owner seeking an early Arthur DeFever passagemaker.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mechanical parts can be supported, but hull, deck and joinery work requires wooden-boat expertise.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Extremely scarce; surviving boats are individual historic vessels.
intelligence.characterNarrative: An early wooden Arthur DeFever passagemaker from the pre-fiberglass era, built in Japan with deep-displacement proportions, tri-cabin accommodation and economical single-diesel propulsion. It belongs to DeFever's original offshore-cruising lineage rather than the later Taiwanese fiberglass trawlers.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: The single-diesel machinery can be exceptionally economical, but wooden-hull ownership is specialist work. Planking, frames, fastenings, decks and insurance availability matter more than engine complexity, and every surviving boat should be treated as an individual historic vessel.
designLineage: Arthur DeFever's earliest private cruising designs were full-displacement 38–54-foot boats created for the Offshore Cruising Society in the 1960s.
Many early examples were built of wood in Japan by yards including Oriental Boat Company.
Surviving boats are documented as DeFever 38 Passagemakers / 38 tri-cabins; DeFever Cruisers separately tracks them as 'DF38 Wood'.
This 38 should not be conflated with the later fiberglass 40/41 trawlers even though owners sometimes describe those hull families as closely related.

intelligence.signature: Low-profile hard-chine twin-diesel DeFever built for materially higher coastal cruising speeds.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Combine traditional two-cabin DeFever accommodation with semi-displacement performance and modernized 1980s styling.
intelligence.idealOwner: A buyer wanting DeFever build/layout values without accepting 7-knot-only performance.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Perkins/Caterpillar components remain supportable; model-specific trim and teak are age-dependent.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Very limited production and used availability.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A low-profile, hard-chine DeFever double-cabin cruiser that departs from the brand's classic swept-sheer displacement look. Twin diesels and a semi-displacement hull give it genuine 12–15-knot cruising capability while retaining full walkaround decks and traditional teak accommodation.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: More performance-oriented than classic DeFevers and normally twin-engine, so fuel burn and machinery maintenance are materially higher. The payoff is useful cruising speed, full walkaround decks and good engine access; teak and 1980s systems remain major refit variables.
designLineage: Powerboat Guide documents the 40 Offshore Cruiser from 1984–1991.
The model was built by CTF in Taiwan on a solid-fiberglass hard-chine semi-displacement hull.
It is distinct from the earlier full-displacement DeFever 40 Passagemaker produced in the 1970s.
The prior B-Atlas '40 Euro' label was unsupported for this record and has been corrected to the documented 40 Offshore Cruiser identity.

evidence.claim: Model identity, character and lineage researched from Powerboat Guide, DeFever Cruisers design/history archives and model-specific records.

intelligence.signature: Classic Taiwan trunk-cabin DeFever with two staterooms, wide decks and single/twin diesel flexibility.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Deliver safe, economical long-range coastal cruising with maximum practical interior volume and traditional teak finish.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple wanting a classic aft-cabin trawler with strong owner-community knowledge.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong owner knowledge and mainstream engine support; aging teak, windows and tanks may require custom work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: One of the more common smaller DeFevers.
intelligence.characterNarrative: One of the archetypal Taiwan-built DeFever trawlers: a two-stateroom trunk-cabin cruiser with wide bulwarked side decks, deep prop-protecting keel, richly finished teak interior and either economical single-diesel or twin-Lehman propulsion.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Excellent liveaboard value and very economical in single-engine form, with secure decks and useful storage. Exterior teak, old tanks, windows and decades of electrical/plumbing modifications can create substantial refit work; twin-engine examples add machinery complexity.
designLineage: The DeFever 41 was built in Taiwan from 1980–1995, first by Miracle Marine and later by Bluewater Marine.
Arthur DeFever regarded the 38/40/41 size family as closely related in concept, but the fiberglass 41 has its own documented production identity.
At least two interior arrangements were offered, both with two private staterooms and galley aft in the salon.
Single 210-hp Cummins and twin 135-hp Lehman installations are both documented, so engine count is intentionally not fixed in B-Atlas.

intelligence.signature: Heavy flush-deck full-displacement offshore cruiser with exceptional tankage and engine-room separation.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Prioritize long-range self-sufficiency, deck security and machinery access over speed or compact size.
intelligence.idealOwner: A long-range cruising couple comfortable with very slow speed and large-vessel maintenance.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Lehman mechanical support is good; large vintage tanks, teak and structure dominate refit exposure.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Finite but strongly identifiable classic-DeFever fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A distinctive flush-deck, full-displacement DeFever designed for genuine offshore range: two private staterooms separated by a near-standing engine room, enormous tankage, single-level side/aft decks and twin Lehman diesels cruising at seven to eight knots.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Extremely capable for slow long-range cruising, with more than 1,000 gallons of fuel and 500 gallons of water, but that capability comes with 40,000-plus pounds of boat and extensive teak. Tank integrity, deck condition, twin-engine systems and haul-out infrastructure are major ownership considerations.
designLineage: The 43 Trawler was produced from 1978–1981 and is one of DeFever's unusual flush-deck designs.
Its aft deck and side decks are on one level rather than using the raised aft-cabin/sundeck arrangement common to many Taiwan trawlers.
The galley-aft salon arrangement reflects Arthur DeFever's preference for keeping food preparation close to outdoor living spaces.
The model is a distinct full-displacement offshore cruiser and not a renamed 41.

intelligence.signature: Later raised-pilothouse DeFever with Portuguese bridge and efficient twin-diesel passage speed.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Modernize traditional DeFever passagemaking ergonomics while retaining conservative speed and protected deck circulation.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting a more modern DeFever with true pilothouse watchkeeping and protected decks.
intelligence.partsAvailability: John Deere-era machinery and modern systems are broadly supportable; builder-specific items are less problematic than on older boats.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but recognizable 2000s used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A later-generation DeFever raised-pilothouse cruiser with Portuguese bridge, protected side decks and a split-level two-stateroom interior. It modernizes the brand's long-range owner-operator formula while retaining conservative eight-to-ten-knot twin-diesel performance.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A more modern and serviceable DeFever than the 1970s/80s trawlers, with protected decks and good passage-making ergonomics. Twin engines, generator, thrusters and substantial domestic systems still make ownership yacht-scale.
designLineage: The documented DeFever 45 Pilothouse was produced from 2002–2008.
It belongs to DeFever's later POCTA-era pilothouse branch rather than the earlier aft-cabin Offshore Cruiser family.
DeFever Cruisers notes that later 45/46/48 pilothouse and Euro variants share closely related hull architecture.
The 45 Pilothouse should remain distinct from the separate DeFever 45 Aft Cabin design.

intelligence.signature: Performance Offshore Cruiser combining DeFever liveaboard layout with 12–14-knot semi-displacement speed.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Increase speed dramatically without abandoning protective keel, wide decks or long-range cruising accommodation.
intelligence.idealOwner: A liveaboard cruiser wanting DeFever character with substantially more speed and three-cabin space.
intelligence.partsAvailability: CAT systems remain supportable; fully cored hull and complex hotel systems demand careful inspection.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Rare; only about a dozen built.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A Performance Offshore Cruiser rather than a traditional slow trawler: the 47 POC uses a wide, fully cored semi-displacement hull, hard aft chines and substantially more horsepower to deliver 12–14-knot cruising while retaining DeFever's protected keel, wide decks and liveaboard interior.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Far more complex and fuel-intensive than the classic single-diesel DeFevers, with twin higher-output diesels, three-stateroom systems and a large enclosed aft deck. Fully cored hull construction also makes moisture inspection especially important.
designLineage: POC means Performance Offshore Cruiser, a faster DeFever branch developed in the mid-1980s in response to buyers wanting more speed.
The 47 POC was built by Sen Koh in Taiwan from 1986–1992.
It followed the same performance-oriented design movement as the 51 POC and related 53/57 POC models.
Only about a dozen 47 POC yachts were built, making it a distinct and relatively scarce model.

intelligence.signature: Cockpit-equipped 44+5 derivative with huge master, walk-in engine room and long-range tankage.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Add practical cockpit/water access to the proven DeFever 44 flush-deck platform without sacrificing owner accommodations.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting a large liveaboard DeFever with cockpit utility and excellent machinery access.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mainstream diesel support and strong DeFever owner network; sheer size and vintage systems drive costs.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Popular within the DeFever community despite limited overall production.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The highly practical cockpit evolution of the DeFever 44 family: a heavy flush-deck cruiser with single-level walkaround decks, huge aft master, near-standing engine room and five feet of added cockpit for line handling, fishing and water access.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Excellent couple's liveaboard layout and exceptionally practical deck access, with low-speed twin-diesel economy and major tankage. At roughly 54,000 pounds with 1,100 gallons of fuel, dockage, haul-out and system maintenance are firmly large-yacht responsibilities.
designLineage: The DeFever 49 Cockpit Motor Yacht is commonly called the '44+5' because it is based on the DeFever 44 with a five-foot cockpit extension.
Production ran from 1994–2006.
The extension also lengthened shafts/rudders and increased waterline length and fuel capacity.
The 49 CMY is therefore a legitimate derivative model, not a duplicate 44 listing.

intelligence.signature: Classic Cape Dory single-engine flybridge power cruiser built on the successful 28 semi-displacement hull.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Combine lobster-boat hull character, protected propulsion and yacht-quality interior in a compact cruising boat.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting a classic New England cruiser with both lower and upper helms.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mainstream Volvo/gas-engine components vary by installation; Cape Dory owner documentation is unusually strong.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Large relative to other Cape Dory power models; most familiar used-market Cape Dory powerboat.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The best-known Cape Dory powerboat: a compact New England flybridge cruiser with a lobster-boat-derived semi-displacement hull, full protective keel, single inboard and unusually yacht-like teak interior for 28 feet.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A mechanically simple classic cruiser with protected single-shaft propulsion and good deck access. Core moisture, windows, aging tanks, old Volvo/Chrysler installations and flybridge structure are more important ownership variables than system complexity.
designLineage: The Cape Dory 28 power family was introduced in the mid-1980s as the company's first major pleasure-power line.
Factory literature identifies four related configurations on the same hull: Flybridge Cruiser, Power Cruiser, Open Fisherman and 280 Sport.
The Flybridge Cruiser adds an upper helm to the enclosed Power Cruiser arrangement and became the best-known version.
More than 220 Cape Dory 28 powerboats were built across the family, representing roughly three-quarters of Cape Dory's pleasure-power production.

intelligence.signature: Open-cockpit fishing/cruising version of the Cape Dory 28 hull.

intelligence.idealOwner: A buyer prioritizing fishing, day use and cockpit space but still wanting overnight capability.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Generic single-inboard systems are supportable; Cape Dory owner archives aid model-specific restoration.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Established but less common than Flybridge version.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The cockpit-first member of the Cape Dory 28 family: an open Down East fisherman with the same protected semi-displacement hull as the cruisers, but substantially less enclosed superstructure and a large working cockpit.

designLineage: The Open Fisherman shares the Cape Dory 28 hull with the Flybridge Cruiser, Power Cruiser and 280 Sport.
Factory and later Newport literature also use Open Sportsman terminology for this open-cockpit configuration.
The Open retains V-berths, a compact galley and enclosed head despite its fishing-oriented deck arrangement.
It is a genuine factory configuration rather than a stripped Flybridge Cruiser.

intelligence.signature: Lower-helm enclosed Cape Dory 28 without flybridge height or duplication.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Deliver classic 28 cruising accommodations with simpler topside structure and lower air draft.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting enclosed steering and classic Downeast styling without a flybridge.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Single-engine systems are straightforward; trim/glazing and core repairs are age-dependent.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Scarcer than Flybridge version but legitimate factory model.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The low-profile enclosed cruiser in the Cape Dory 28 family, combining a lower inside helm, teak-trimmed salon, single protected shaft and the same salty semi-displacement hull without the height or complexity of a flybridge.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A strong choice for buyers who value classic appearance and inside steering but want to avoid a flybridge. Single-engine simplicity keeps running costs modest; age-related core, window, tank and repower work remain the main ownership risks.

The Flybridge Cruiser is the same core cruising concept with an upper helm added.
The 28 Open Fisherman and 280 Sport use the same hull but different deck/cockpit missions.
B-Atlas uses '28 Power Cruiser' to keep this factory powerboat distinct from the unrelated Cape Dory 28 sailboat.

intelligence.idealOwner: A buyer wanting classic Cape Dory finish with substantially more speed than the 28.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Twin Volvo systems remain supportable; short production means model-specific parts and institutional knowledge are limited.

intelligence.characterNarrative: A compact twin-engine Cape Dory PowerYacht designed for substantially more speed than the 28: hard-chine modified-V hull, full-length protective keel, wide 12-foot beam, flybridge and traditional teak interior in a short-lived 30-foot family cruiser.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Twin diesels provide useful high-teens cruising speed, but double machinery count and a 12-foot beam materially raise ownership costs over the 28. The short original production run makes Cape Dory-specific trim and model knowledge less common.
designLineage: The factory called the model the Cape Dory 30 PowerYacht; Powerboat Guide commonly catalogs it as the 30 Flybridge.
It was introduced near the end of Cape Dory's Massachusetts production and only about 15 were built in the original run.
The 30 uses a hard-chine modified-V hull and twin propulsion rather than the 28 family's rounded-bilge semi-displacement formula.
The molds later passed to Nauset Marine, which continued related semi-custom production.

intelligence.designPhilosophy: Provide a manageable couple's cruiser with fast cruising, full side decks and excellent lower-helm visibility.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting a high-quality New England flybridge cruiser in the low-30-foot class.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Twin Volvo-era systems are broadly understood; Cape Dory/Robinhood lineage helps with model knowledge.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Rare but strongly identifiable.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The smaller sister to the Cape Dory 36 PowerYacht: a handsome Clive Dent-designed twin-diesel flybridge cruiser with full-length keel, wide side decks, lower helm and a single private forward stateroom.

designLineage: Cape Dory introduced the 33 PowerYacht in 1988 as a smaller companion to the established 36.
Factory history records 22 Cape Dory-built examples; Powerboat Guide tracks the broader 1988–1994 production lineage through the Newport Shipyards transition.
The 33 uses the same New England-style modified-V, protective-keel design philosophy as the 30 and 36 PowerYachts.
Robinhood Marine later produced the design under license as the Robinhood 33.

intelligence.designPhilosophy: Provide family cruising space and 20-knot performance while preserving Cape Dory construction, keel protection and teak craftsmanship.
intelligence.personality: Substantial, traditional and faster than it looks.
intelligence.idealOwner: A family or couple wanting classic appearance with twin-engine coastal performance.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Major engines/systems are supportable; Cape Dory-specific joinery and aging structures require specialist work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small production fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: Cape Dory's larger two-stateroom PowerYacht: a broad-beam twin-engine Downeast flybridge cruiser with modified-V hull, long protective keel and substantial teak interior, designed to combine traditional appearance with roughly 20-knot performance.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A true twin-engine cruising yacht rather than a trawler despite its traditional profile. Good machinery access and protected running gear help, but twin engines, multiple cabins, teak and 1980s systems make annual upkeep substantial.
designLineage: The 36 PowerYacht preceded the 33 and established Cape Dory's larger Clive Dent-designed pleasure-power formula.
Factory documentation covers 1987–1990 Cape Dory production, while technical guides usually catalog the flybridge model as 1988–1990.
A two-stateroom interior was standard, with a one-stateroom/dinette alternative.
The 33 PowerYacht followed as a smaller sister using the same general design language.

intelligence.signature: Flagship Cape Dory/Newport Explorer with twin diesels, two helms and two-stateroom cruising accommodations.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Create a fast-trawler/Explorer flagship that preserves New England styling, protected running gear and quality joinery.
intelligence.idealOwner: A serious cruising couple wanting traditional styling but flexible trawler-to-high-teens speeds.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Caterpillar 3116 support remains broad; model-specific components and cored structure require careful survey.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Very limited production but high model distinctiveness.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The final and largest Cape Dory/Newport pleasure-power design: a 40-foot Explorer with modified-V hull, full keel, twin diesels, lower helm, flybridge and two private staterooms, able to cruise either economically at trawler speeds or in the high teens.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Large, comfortable and flexible in speed, but twin Caterpillar diesels, 400 gallons of fuel, two heads and a flybridge make this a full yacht-scale ownership proposition. Cored hullsides and decks deserve careful moisture inspection.
designLineage: Hull #1 of the Cape Dory 40 powerboat was built in 1992 after Newport Shipyards acquired the Cape Dory name and most powerboat designs.
The 40 Explorer was designed by Clive Dent as the flagship of the later Cape Dory/Newport PowerYacht line.
It preserves the protective keel and New England styling of the smaller 30/33/36 boats while increasing accommodation to two staterooms and two heads.
The 40 Explorer is a fast Explorer/Downeast cruiser rather than a conventional full-displacement trawler.

intelligence.signature: Soft-chined sail-derived trawler hull with twin low-output diesels and exceptional low-speed economy.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Reuse a proven ballasted motorsailer hull as a dedicated power cruiser, emphasizing seakindliness and economy rather than volume or speed.
intelligence.idealOwner: A buyer who values slow economical cruising and sailboat-like hull behavior more than beam or modern interior volume.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Perkins-era engines are well understood, but Gulfstar-specific interior/structural parts are mostly custom restoration items.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but recognizable classic-trawler used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: An unusual American trawler built on the same soft-chined, ballasted semi-displacement hull as Gulfstar's 36 Motorsailer. Twin small Perkins diesels, a deep keel and moderate beam make it a slow, economical powerboat with distinctly sailboat-like hull behavior rather than a conventional boxy Taiwan trawler.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Exceptionally economical at 7–8 knots and mechanically simple despite twin engines because the original Perkins installations are low-output. Age, ballast/keel structure, old tanks, windows, decks and insurance on a 50-year-old boat matter more than performance machinery.
designLineage: The Gulfstar 36 Trawler was produced from 1972–1976 on the same hull used for the Gulfstar 36 Motorsailer.
The powerboat identity is legitimate: the Trawler received twin diesels, powerboat deck/helm arrangements and no dependence on a sailing rig.
In 1975 Gulfstar introduced the 36 Mk II with a raised aft deck, full-beam master, enlarged flybridge, larger rudders and redesigned teak interior.
The 36 Trawler and 36 Motorsailer therefore share hull lineage but remain materially different factory configurations and B-Atlas scopes.

intelligence.signature: Large sail-derived Gulfstar trawler with long keel, rounded bilges and Mk II sundeck evolution.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Scale the same low-speed, seakindly concept into greater liveaboard room while retaining protected running gear and moderate beam.
intelligence.idealOwner: A liveaboard cruising couple comfortable at nine knots and willing to maintain a large 1970s yacht.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mechanical systems are conventional, but vintage teak, tanks, windows and interior components often require custom work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Limited but established used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A long, moderate-beam Gulfstar trawler using essentially the Gulfstar 43 Motorsailer hull without the sailing rig. Its rounded bilges, long deep keel and twin Perkins diesels produce seakindly nine-knot cruising, while the Mk II sundeck version adds the larger aft master associated with later motor yachts.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A comfortable and efficient offshore-oriented cruiser at displacement-like speeds, with protected running gear and useful engine-room access. Twin machinery, extensive teak, aging tanks and large vintage systems make ownership materially more demanding than the 36.
designLineage: The Gulfstar 43 Trawler was produced from 1972–1977 on the Gulfstar 43 Motorsailer hull.
The original version used a traditional trunk-cabin arrangement.
A 1975 Mk II redesign added a full-width aft deck, revised flybridge and larger master stateroom, along with a full teak interior.
The 43 remains a valid powerboat despite its sail-derived hull; the motorsailer is a separate configuration outside this B-Atlas record.

intelligence.signature: Motor-yacht-shaped Gulfstar that still operates like a displacement trawler.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Package full liveaboard motor-yacht accommodations around a deep-keel, low-speed hull and modest twin diesels.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting aft-deck motor-yacht living with trawler-like fuel economy rather than speed.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Perkins systems remain supportable; large vintage domestic systems and Gulfstar-specific joinery dominate refit exposure.
intelligence.marketAvailability: About 105 built, giving it meaningful model recognition.
intelligence.characterNarrative: Gulfstar's transition into the modern motor-yacht market: a heavy deep-keel Motor Cruiser that looks like a conventional aft-deck motor yacht but behaves like a trawler, cruising around 8½ knots on modest twin Perkins diesels.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A substantial two-stateroom liveaboard cruiser with excellent engine-room separation and secure side decks. Twin engines are modestly powered, but 500 gallons of fuel, two heads, generator/air-conditioning spaces and large teak surfaces make restoration and annual upkeep yacht-scale.
designLineage: The 44 Motor Cruiser was introduced in 1978 and produced through 1980.
It marked Gulfstar's move away from the earlier trawlers that directly reused motorsailer hulls and toward purpose-developed motor-yacht products.
The deep-keel hull is displacement-oriented and the standard 130-hp Perkins twins deliver trawler-speed performance despite the motor-yacht profile.
The later Gulfstar 48/49 Motor Yacht family developed the enclosed-aft-deck motor-yacht concept further and should not be conflated with this 44.

intelligence.signature: Three-stateroom enclosed-aft-deck Gulfstar with true semi-displacement motor-yacht performance.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Evolve Gulfstar's motor-yacht architecture into a large all-weather salon and higher-speed cruising platform.
intelligence.idealOwner: A liveaboard or cruising family prepared for full large-yacht costs and systems.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Perkins/Detroit machinery remains supportable; cored hull, HVAC, laundry and extensive hotel systems increase complexity.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Limited but clearly documented late-Gulfstar used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A large three-stateroom Gulfstar motor yacht whose enclosed, air-conditioned aft deck becomes the main salon. Twin high-output diesels, semi-displacement hull and small line-handling cockpit give it genuine 12–17-knot cruising capability while retaining a long keel and traditional Gulfstar teak interior.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A true large-yacht proposition: three staterooms, three heads, walk-in engine room, laundry, large generator/air-conditioning loads and twin 350–435 hp diesels. Balsa-cored hull construction makes moisture history particularly important in addition to machinery and tank condition.
designLineage: The Gulfstar 49 Motor Yacht was produced from 1984–1987.
It was an evolutionary refinement of Gulfstar's 48-footer built from 1981–1983.
The defining change is the fully enclosed aft deck used as the main salon, with the mid-level deckhouse devoted to galley and dinette.
The 49 belongs to Gulfstar's later performance motor-yacht lineage and is distinct from the slower 44 Motor Cruiser and earlier sail-derived trawlers.

intelligence.signature: American-built fast-trawler precursor that can cruise efficiently at seven knots or plane with larger diesels.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Combine trawler accommodations and economy with a modified-V hull and enough horsepower flexibility to eliminate the traditional trawler's speed limitation.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting classic trawler appearance, wide decks and flexible speed without extensive exterior teak.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Engines and general marine systems remain supportable by component maker; Californian-specific mahogany joinery, windows and legacy hardware may require custom work.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Strong recognition among West Coast and classic-trawler buyers; more than 200 were produced.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A distinctly American answer to the 1970s Taiwan trawler: the Californian 34 LRC combines traditional trawler styling and excellent low-speed economy with a solid-fiberglass modified-V hull capable of true planing speeds when fitted with larger diesels. Wide side decks, a lower helm and surprising two-stateroom availability make it unusually versatile for 34 feet.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A relatively straightforward twin-shaft cruiser with strong fiberglass construction and very little exterior teak. Engine packages vary dramatically, so a low-powered Perkins boat and a Caterpillar-powered fast cruiser have very different fuel, performance and maintenance profiles; decks, windows, tanks and decades of owner modifications remain major survey items.
designLineage: Jule Marshall and Myrna Elliott developed Californian Yachts around the idea of building faster, moderately priced American trawler-style cruisers rather than copying slow Asian imports.
The 34 LRC followed the successful 42 LRC and became one of Californian's best-known models, with more than 200 built during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Unlike most traditional trawlers, the 34 uses a modified-V hull with nearly flat aft sections, allowing either 7-knot economical operation with small diesels or roughly 16–20-knot cruising with larger engine packages.
The larger 38 LRC Sedan continues the same trawler-profile/modified-V design philosophy rather than representing a fundamentally different brand branch.

intelligence.signature: Large sedan LRC combining trawler circulation and mahogany interior with genuine modified-V fast-cruiser performance.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Scale the 34 LRC concept into greater cockpit, salon and stateroom volume while retaining wide decks and flexible low-to-high-speed operation.
intelligence.personality: Roomy, capable and distinctly West Coast.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple or small family wanting sedan-trawler usability with the option for substantially more speed.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Caterpillar/Perkins and generic marine systems remain broadly supportable; model-specific cabinetry, glazing and hardware are legacy items.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Popular in its era and still regularly visible in the North American used market.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The larger sedan expression of Californian's LRC formula: a broad 13-foot-beam trawler-profile cruiser with wide side decks, lower helm, large cockpit and solid-fiberglass modified-V hull capable of everything from economical displacement-speed running to nearly 20-knot cruising with higher-output Caterpillar diesels.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A strong liveaboard/coastal-cruising layout with excellent deck access and minimal exterior wood compared with many contemporaries. Twin engines, 400 gallons of fuel and 28,000 pounds of boat make it materially more expensive to own than the 34, while machinery choice can shift performance from trawler-like economy to fast-cruiser fuel consumption.
designLineage: The 38 LRC Sedan was produced from 1978–1985 as the larger companion to the Californian 34 LRC.
It preserves the 34's defining combination of trawler appearance, mahogany interior, broad side decks and a modified-V hull capable of much higher speeds than conventional displacement trawlers.
Single- and twin-stateroom layouts were offered, both using a galley-up sedan arrangement and standard lower helm.
The 38 LRC Sedan should not be conflated with later Californian 38 Convertibles or Motor Yachts, which belong to different model families.

intelligence.signature: American-built under-30-foot Hargrave trawler with unusually broad beam and single-diesel economy.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Create a safe, fuel-miserly extended-cruising boat under 30 feet without sacrificing interior livability.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple who values room and low fuel burn over speed or road portability.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Original Perkins installations are well understood and many boats have mainstream repowers; Prairie-specific trim and hardware are legacy/custom items.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small surviving fleet but active owner interest and identifiable hull history.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A compact American-built Jack Hargrave trawler created specifically to fill the late-1970s gap for an economical, genuinely livable cruiser under 30 feet. Its semi-displacement hull, full keel, very wide 12-foot beam and single Perkins diesel deliver exceptional interior volume and 6–7-knot fuel economy.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Very simple mechanically and exceptionally economical, usually with one small diesel and protected shaft. The unusually broad beam provides excellent interior room but prevents normal road trailering; after nearly five decades, tanks, decks, windows, wiring and repower quality matter far more than original engine specification.
designLineage: Prairie Boat Works commissioned J.B. Hargrave in 1977 to design a semi-displacement trawler under 30 feet; production began in 1978.
The 29 Coastal Cruiser became Prairie's defining powerboat and used a rounded-bottom/soft-chine semi-displacement hull with full keel.
The success of the 29 directly led Prairie to commission the larger 36 Coastal Cruiser using the same broad design philosophy.
When Prairie closed in early 1982, Atlantic Yachts acquired the molds and tooling and reintroduced the 29 lineage as the Atlantic 30.

intelligence.signature: Two-stateroom Hargrave trawler whose hull lived on for another decade as the Atlantic 37.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Scale the Prairie 29's economical semi-displacement/full-keel formula into genuine liveaboard accommodations with two private cabins and heads.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple planning extended coastal, Great Loop or liveaboard use and comfortable maintaining twin-diesel systems.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Conventional Perkins/Cummins/Lehman-era systems plus direct Atlantic 37 lineage provide unusually good knowledge continuity for a defunct small builder.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Limited but recognizable; the Atlantic 37 successor makes the broader hull family more common.
intelligence.characterNarrative: The larger Jack Hargrave development of the Prairie 29 concept: a beamy American-built double-cabin semi-displacement trawler with full keel, twin diesels, two private heads with separate showers and unusually generous liveaboard accommodations for 36 feet.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A comfortable Great Loop/coastal liveaboard platform with protected running gear, shallow draft and excellent machinery access. Twin engines, two heads, large tankage and 22,000 pounds of boat increase upkeep, but systems remain conventional and the direct Atlantic 37 continuation helps preserve owner knowledge and parts solutions.
designLineage: Prairie introduced the 36 Coastal Cruiser in 1979 after the strong reception of the Prairie 29.
The 36 retained the 29's soft-chine semi-displacement/full-keel design language while adding a true two-stateroom, two-head interior.
Prairie produced the 36 until early 1982, when the company closed.
Atlantic Yachts acquired the tooling and reintroduced the same hull in 1982 as the Atlantic 37 Double Cabin, creating a direct Prairie 36 → Atlantic 37 lineage.

intelligence.signature: Long-running Ed Monk Jr. aft-cabin trawler with single-diesel economy and unusually strong owner support.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Prioritize safe deck circulation, two-cabin liveaboard comfort, protected running gear and economical single-engine cruising in a manageable 36-foot hull.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple seeking a classic Great Loop/coastal trawler with separate guest cabin, secure side decks and simple machinery.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong owner-community knowledge and mainstream Lehman, Perkins and Cummins support; early exterior teak and model-specific joinery require more hands-on maintenance.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Large by classic-trawler standards, with more than 250 built and regular North American used-market availability.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A classic Ed Monk Jr.-designed aft-cabin trawler that became one of the most recognizable North American cruising boats of the 1980s and 1990s. Its semi-displacement hull, full skeg/keel protection, single diesel, wide side decks and two-stateroom layout combine simple low-speed economy with unusually comfortable long-term cruising for 36 feet.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: One of the simpler 36-foot liveaboard trawlers to operate: normally one shaft-drive diesel, straightforward systems, secure walkaround decks and strong owner knowledge. Early Taiwan boats carry much more exterior teak and may have older Lehman/Perkins installations; later Nova Scotia boats reduce wood maintenance but often add more powerful Cummins machinery and modern cruising systems.
designLineage: Ed Monk Jr., not Ed Monk Sr., designed the Monk 36; the two naval architects worked together for many years, which likely contributes to recurring attribution confusion.
Production began in Taiwan in 1982 and shifted to Nova Scotia in 1992 while retaining the same essential hull and galley-up aft-cabin arrangement.
The post-1992 Canadian-built generation reduced exterior teak, eliminated the aft-head bathtub and improved the aft master berth placement.
Production continued through 2007, with more than 250 boats reported built over roughly 25 years.

intelligence.signature: Documented Canadian-market Oceania sedan trawler, not an Ocean Alexander.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Maximize protected walkaround deck space, interior teak and liveaboard room around a low-powered single-diesel trawler hull.
intelligence.idealOwner: A classic-trawler buyer comfortable with a scarce marque and restoration-oriented ownership.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Ford Lehman and generic marine systems remain supportable; Oceania-specific parts and documentation are scarce.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Very rare; surviving examples are difficult to identify.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A Canadian-market Taiwan-built sedan trawler from 1980, combining broad covered walkaround decks, an unusually teak-rich interior and a single Ford Lehman diesel in a roomy 36-foot cruising package. It is a separate Oceania Yachts identity, not an Ocean Alexander model.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Single-engine simplicity and excellent sheltered deck circulation make the boat attractive for slow cruising. Extensive teak, vintage deckhouse construction, old tanks/windows and the rarity of the Oceania marque make condition and prior restoration more important than model-specific parts availability.
designLineage: Canadian Yachting tested the first Oceania 36 Sedan imported to Canada in 1980 by Donaldson Yacht Sales of Port Credit, Ontario.
The boat was marketed under the Oceania Yachts name as part of a range of Oriental trawlers; available companion configurations included aft-cabin styles.
Its U.S.-origin design and Taiwan construction reflect the broad late-1970s/early-1980s trawler-import market rather than Ocean Alexander's documented model lineage.

B-Atlas corrected the prior Ocean Alexander attribution because exact-model research found no credible historical Ocean Alexander 36 Sedan, while contemporary documentation clearly establishes the Oceania 36 Sedan.

intelligence.signature: Early Ocean Alexander twin-diesel flybridge sedan with two-stateroom teak interior.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Combine Taiwanese craftsmanship and Pacific Northwest cruising practicality in a broad, moderate-speed sedan hull.
intelligence.idealOwner: A couple wanting classic Ocean Alexander quality in a relatively compact flybridge sedan.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mainstream diesel systems are supportable; exact original fittings and tankage vary heavily after decades of refits.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Rare but verified 1985–86 used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: An early Ocean Alexander flybridge sedan from the mid-1980s, built around a broad modified-V hull, twin shaft diesels, two private staterooms and the teak joinery that established the brand's Pacific Northwest reputation.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A comfortable Pacific Northwest cruising platform with twin diesels, upper/lower helms and high-quality teak interior work. Repowers and swim-platform/hull extensions are common enough that machinery, actual LOA, tankage and weight should be verified on each boat.
designLineage: Verified surviving 1985 and 1986 boats establish the Ocean Alexander 39 Sedan as a real production model.
The 39 predates the later, better-documented 42 Sedan and larger Classico/Pilothouse lines.
Period examples use a 39-foot hull/deck length with appendages or later owner-added extensions sometimes producing 42-foot-plus overall measurements.
The model remains separate from the later Ocean Alexander 42 Sedan; no evidence supports treating the 39 simply as a renamed 42.

intelligence.signature: Late-1980s Tollycraft two-stateroom Sport Sedan with strong PNW cruising pedigree.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Provide open-plan family accommodations and good rough-water performance in a solid-fiberglass modified-V sedan.
intelligence.idealOwner: A family or couple wanting a classic Northwest flybridge cruiser rather than a slow trawler.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong Tollycraft owner support and mainstream gas/diesel components.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Common by classic-PNW standards.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A quintessential Pacific Northwest family cruiser: solid-fiberglass modified-V hull, twin inboards, lower helm, roomy two-stateroom interior and a practical cockpit/flybridge arrangement designed for year-round coastal use rather than trawler-speed economy.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Solid fiberglass construction and conventional twin inboards make the structure and machinery understandable, but twin engines, flybridge systems and aging fuel/electrical installations create normal 34-foot motor-yacht upkeep. Gas and diesel examples have materially different operating economics.
designLineage: The 34 Sport Sedan was produced from 1987–1993.
It is a later model than Tollycraft's earlier 34 Sedan and should not be conflated with the 1972–1980 generation.
Two flybridge arrangements were offered for different regional preferences: helm-aft for East Coast buyers and helm-forward for Pacific buyers.
Fuel capacity increased after the first production year, so 200- and 296-gallon specifications both legitimately appear.

intelligence.signature: Heavier 1970s Tollycraft sedan with broad beam and strong rough-water reputation.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Prioritize robust fiberglass construction, interior volume and conventional twin-shaft cruising for Northwest waters.
intelligence.idealOwner: A hands-on owner wanting a classic PNW sedan with good parts/community knowledge.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Excellent owner-community knowledge; repowered machinery varies widely.
intelligence.marketAvailability: About 150 built; persistent PNW used fleet.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A heavy, broad-beam Pacific Northwest sedan cruiser from Tollycraft's 1970s era, combining a modified-V hull, twin direct-drive engines, large salon windows and practical flybridge/cockpit circulation in a boat renowned for rough-water confidence.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: A rugged, straightforward cruiser with excellent owner-community support and conventional shaft machinery. Nearly every surviving boat has decades of upgrades, so repower quality, fuel tanks, wiring, windows and deck hardware matter more than factory engine specification.
designLineage: Surviving market records and the Canadian Tollycruisers fleet archive establish the 37 Sedan as a distinct Tollycraft model, with about 150 built.
Verified examples span 1974–1980.
The 37 belongs to Tollycraft's older sedan/convertible generation and is not the same model as the later 34 Sport Sedan.
Gasoline and diesel propulsion are both common in the surviving fleet, with many boats repowered during their long service lives.

intelligence.signature: Full-displacement Universal Marine tri-cabin with common single-Lehman configuration.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Deliver maximum teak-lined liveaboard accommodation and low-speed economy in a traditional Taiwan trawler layout.
intelligence.idealOwner: A buyer seeking classic trawler character and willing to manage vintage teak/deck systems.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Lehman and generic systems remain supportable; builder-specific woodwork and fittings require custom solutions.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Small but identifiable fleet under multiple distributor names.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A heavily built Taiwanese full-displacement tri-cabin trawler with two private sleeping cabins, two heads, extensive teak and the classic single Ford Lehman 120 installation that defined economical 1970s cruising.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Very economical and simple in single-Lehman form, with a spacious teak interior and strong full-displacement cruising character. Original teak decks, deckhouse leaks, black-iron tanks, old wiring and extensive woodwork are the primary age-related ownership exposures.
designLineage: Verified 1977–1981 boats were built by Universal Marine Co. Ltd. in Taipei, Taiwan.
The design appears under both Universal Marine and distributor/secondary names such as Litton, reflecting common private-label practice among Taiwanese builders of the era.
Universal Marine later became associated with construction of early Ocean Alexander yachts, but the Universal 36 remains a distinct builder/model identity.
Single- and twin-engine examples exist; B-Atlas represents the common single-Lehman tri-cabin configuration while leaving listing-specific machinery authoritative.

intelligence.designPhilosophy: Blend Europa weather protection, teak-lined accommodation and low-speed efficiency in a 40-foot Taiwan trawler.
intelligence.idealOwner: A cruising couple prioritizing protected side decks and simple single-shaft operation.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Mechanical support is straightforward; original deck, tank and superstructure work is restoration-intensive.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Rare and inconsistently labeled.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A classic 1970s Universal Marine Europa trawler with a single Ford Lehman diesel, long covered side decks and a teak-rich interior, combining the practical weather protection of a sedan/Europa layout with slow, economical shaft-drive cruising.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Single-Lehman operation is economical and mechanically simple, but a 40-foot teak-decked Taiwan trawler carries substantial restoration exposure. designLineage: Verified 1977 Universal Marine Europa examples establish a distinct approximately 40-foot model.
Period and surviving records also use Pacific 38/Pacific 40 or generic Universal Trawler wording, illustrating inconsistent distributor naming rather than necessarily different hulls.
The Europa's long covered side decks and sedan-oriented superstructure distinguish it from Universal's tri-cabin 36.
Because factory documentation is scarce, B-Atlas uses Universal Marine 40 Europa as the canonical searchable identity while retaining Pacific/Universal Trawler names as aliases.

intelligence.signature: Long-lived PNW aft-cabin motor yacht that became a Chris-Craft Catalina after Uniflite closed.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Maximize private-cabin family cruising space on a robust modified-V hull with conventional twin inboards.
intelligence.personality: Solid, practical and distinctly Pacific Northwest.
intelligence.idealOwner: A family or couple wanting classic aft-cabin comfort and willing to manage twin-engine fuel and aging systems.
intelligence.partsAvailability: Strong Uniflite owner knowledge plus mainstream gas/diesel systems; model-specific trim is legacy.
intelligence.marketAvailability: Large surviving fleet for its era.
intelligence.characterNarrative: A durable Pacific Northwest aft-cabin motor yacht built around Uniflite's solid-fiberglass modified-V 36-foot hull. Its full-width aft master, lower helm, wide side decks and twin inboards made it an early high-volume family cruiser rather than a trawler, with gasoline performance commonly near 18 knots.
intelligence.ownershipCharacter: Straightforward twin-shaft machinery and solid early hull construction are positives, but these boats are now old enough that fuel tanks, wiring, windows, decks and prior repowers dominate condition. Uniflite's well-known blister problems require hull and topside inspection, especially on later fire-retardant-resin boats.
designLineage: The Uniflite 36 Double Cabin was produced from 1972 through 1984 on the same basic solid-fiberglass hull as the 36 Sport Sedan.
In 1984 Uniflite introduced a 36 II with a fully cored hull, revised flybridge and updated interior; this was a late-generation evolution within the 36 Double Cabin line.
When Uniflite closed in 1984, Chris-Craft acquired the molds and continued the design as the Catalina 36/362/370 family.
A cockpit derivative, the Uniflite 41 Yacht Fisherman, was created by extending the same aft-cabin concept with a working cockpit.

intelligence.signature: Long-running Great Lakes/Pennsylvania-built tri-cabin family motor yacht with exceptional space for 36 feet.
intelligence.designPhilosophy: Use an aft-cabin layout and large bridge to create privacy and social space at an accessible production-boat price.
intelligence.idealOwner: A freshwater/coastal cruiser who values accommodation over fuel economy and accepts twin-engine ownership.
